findings.summary: Status lines show priority only when it is not normal, but the request asks status to show each request's priority.
findings.evidence: Request: 'athena plan and athena status show each request's priority.' The plan's display.rs test asserts that a normal line has no priority suffix. job_line (status.rs:512) builds lines for every job, including jobs that have no request. Fix: Either show 'priority normal' on status lines for jobs that have request text and leave it off only for jobs without a request, or keep the suffix-only design and state it in the CHANGELOG and decisions.md entries as a deliberate reading of 'show', so the owner can overrule it.

findings.summary: Restricting each wave to the best-priority items changes which items can be grouped together when priorities differ, so it touches the out-of-scope grouping in effect.
findings.evidence: plan.rs:192-202 groups only within the ready set, so a smaller wave means fewer items run in parallel. The plan names this risk, but no test covers grouping when priorities are mixed. Fix: Add one test for mixed priorities that asserts the resulting groups: the high item and its prerequisite each sit in their own group ahead of the normal group. Also note the reduced grouping in the decisions.md entry.
findings.location: Decision 1 / Out of scope 'Changing the parallel grouping logic'

findings.summary: The new no-priority test is written after the change, so it cannot be shown to fail first. What actually guards today's order is the existing tests passing unchanged.
findings.evidence: 'Fails without the behavior: If the default order changed, the no-priority test and the existing tests fail.' Fix: Name in the demonstration the existing plan.rs and drain.rs tests that pin today's order, so the evidence points at tests that existed before the change.

summary: I read plan.rs, reading.rs plan_entry, status.rs job_line, display.rs plan and drain.rs. The code the plan relies on exists as it describes. Plan::build (plan.rs:160-214) builds waves of ready items and sorts each by (rung, age) at line 191. reading::plan_entry already has the request text (reading.rs:1511), and job_line can reach the same `job.request`. display::plan has an entry_lines closure where a priority line fits. The drain works plan.groups in order (drain.rs:1154), so a change in wave order reaches the drain. I traced the effective-priority wave rule through demonstration 2's case (h is high and depends on n1; n2 and n3 are unrelated): it gives [n1], then [h], then [n2, n3]. That matches the asserted exact order. Under the old within-wave sort the order would be different, so the demonstration does test the behavior. With every item at normal priority, the restricted wave is the whole ready set, so today's order and groups stay the same. The cycle check still holds, because a non-empty ready set stays non-empty after the restriction. The edits to main.rs and drain.rs only change help text and module docs, so Athena's two scope findings are minor and justified. There is a second, unrelated JobLine struct in drain.rs (line 436); it is not the status JobLine, so the plan's open question about other constructions is safe. I found nothing that blocks the plan.
